prompt: The client asks: "Should we open restaurants in Texas?" Fact sheet: the Texas market is worth $2B and growing 6% a year; the top three players hold 20% share; each restaurant costs $1.5M and pays back in 3 years; our hurdle is a 4-year payback; we run 50 restaurants in California; our California restaurants' sales grew 2% last year. Which is the best recommendation?

options.text: Don't enter Texas. Each restaurant there costs $1.5M, and our 50 California restaurants still have room to grow profit.
options.feedback: It ignores the deciding fact: each Texas restaurant pays back in 3 years, inside the 4-year hurdle, in a fast-growing, fragmented market.

options.text: Texas looks promising on growth and payback. With no presence there, though, a decision feels premature.
options.feedback: This never commits, even though every number points to entering.

options.text: Enter Texas. Our California sales grew only 2% last year, so we need a new market to grow.
options.feedback: California's growth doesn't make Texas pay. Texas is a $2B market growing 6% a year, and each restaurant pays back in 3 years, inside the 4-year hurdle.

options.text: Enter Texas. The $2B market grows 6% a year, the top three hold only 20%, and each restaurant pays back in 3 years.
options.feedback: Right. It leads with the answer and backs it with market, competition and payback.

explanation: Full answer: Enter Texas. The $2B market grows 6% a year, the top three players hold only 20%, and each restaurant pays back in 3 years against a 4-year hurdle. The main risk is that our California supply chain doesn't stretch to Texas, so the next step is to open 5 restaurants in one city and confirm the payback. What would change the answer: pilot restaurants tracking toward a payback beyond 4 years.

irrelevant_facts: Our California restaurants' sales grew 2% last year.
